items.name: Hoop-house greenhouse (high tunnel)
items.scope: A ground-post hoop house: steel bows on driven ground posts, wood baseboards and hip boards, framed end walls with a door and vents, and greenhouse film. The site prep (level, drained) is in. Heating, electrical and irrigation are separate jobs.

items.name: Chicken coop and run
items.scope: A shed-roof coop on a framed floor, with a people door and a pop door, a roost, nest boxes and vents, and a run wrapped in 1/2 in hardware cloth. Sizes and quantities come from the coop plan (4 sq ft a hen inside, 10 in the run). Power and water lines are separate jobs.

items.name: Workshop on a concrete slab
items.scope: A gable-roofed workshop framed on a concrete slab: the permit, layout, the slab (forms, base, reinforcement, pour, cure), stud walls with a header over the door, rafters, sheathing, underlayment and shingles, and siding. The slab's quantities come from the slab plan and the walls' and roof's from the gable-shed plan. Wiring is its own job.

items.name: Cold room for the harvest (an insulated walk-in cooler)
items.scope: A walk-in cold room framed inside a dry building (the workshop, a barn): insulated walls, ceiling and floor, a sealed vapor retarder on the warm side, a tight insulated door, and a window air conditioner run cold by a controller (CoolBot or similar). Its dedicated circuit is its own job and may need a permit and an electrician.

items.name: A toilet that keeps running
items.scope: Nothing here is dangerous, but shut the water off at the valve behind the toilet before taking anything apart, and lift the tank lid carefully: it's heavy and breaks easily.

items.name: No hot water
items.scope: If you smell gas, stop: leave and call the gas utility from outside. Switch an electric heater off at its breaker before opening any panel on it. Hot water and the relief valve can scald: keep clear of the valve's pipe.

items.name: A breaker that keeps tripping
items.scope: Never take the panel cover off, and reset a breaker no more than once or twice: a breaker that trips again is protecting the wiring. A hot, buzzing or scorched breaker, or a burning smell, means leave it off and call a licensed electrician now.

items.name: Air conditioning that runs but doesn't cool
items.scope: Switch the outdoor unit off at its disconnect (and the breaker) before touching it: its capacitor holds a charge even then, so leave the electrical parts to a technician. Never open the refrigerant lines; that work needs a certified technician.

items.name: A dryer that runs but doesn't heat
items.scope: Unplug the dryer (or switch off its breaker) before opening it: an electric dryer runs on 240 volts. A gas dryer follows the gas rule: a smell of gas means stop and leave. Lint is a fire risk, so clean it out as you go.

items.name: A roof leak
items.scope: Look from the attic and the ground first, and stay off a wet, icy or steep roof: roof work needs fall protection and a second person. Keep water away from light fixtures and wiring below the leak.

opened.name: Chicken coop and run
opened.scope: A shed-roof coop on a framed floor, with a people door and a pop door, a roost, nest boxes and vents, and a run wrapped in 1/2 in hardware cloth. Sizes and quantities come from the coop plan (4 sq ft a hen inside, 10 in the run). Power and water lines are separate jobs.
opened.permit: A coop is usually a small accessory building; many places exempt one under 200 sq ft, but zoning may limit hens, setbacks and roosters. Codes, snow and wind loads, and permit rules vary by place: check with your local building department before you start.
materials: 2x4 framing lumber (treated for the floor frame)
metal roof panels and screws with washers

steps.do: Size it for the flock with the coop plan (4 sq ft a hen inside, 10 in the run), and check how many hens your zoning allows.
Choose high, well-drained ground with afternoon shade and the door away from the prevailing winter wind; leave room to walk all round it to clean.
Call 811 before setting blocks or digging the run apron.
Set level concrete blocks (or treated skids on gravel) at the corners and midspans.
Build the floor frame from treated 2x4s (joists at 16 in), check its diagonals, then glue and screw the plywood floor.
Frame the walls flat on the floor (studs at 24 in), with the people door, the pop door and window openings framed with headers, then stand and brace them.
Set the rafters at 24 in with a 12 in overhang, then the metal roof panels, screwed through the ribs into purlins or rafters.
Side it, and cut vents high on both sides (about 1 sq ft for every 10 birds), covered with hardware cloth.
Frame the run and wrap it in 1/2 in hardware cloth, fastened every few inches with washers or battens.
Bury an apron: hardware cloth 12 in down, or laid 2 ft out flat and pinned, all round the run.
Fit two-step latches on every door and the pop door.
Install the roost (wide face up, 10 in a hen, higher than the nest boxes) and the nest boxes (one per 4 hens, about 12 in cubes, dark and low).
Walk the coop at dusk with a light: any gap bigger than 1/2 in, any loose wire, any latch that gives.

rules.when: digging before the utility lines are located
rules.instead: Stop. Call 811 (in the US) and wait for the marks before you dig.

rules.when: work at height without fall protection, or alone on a roof
rules.instead: Stop. Get a harness and anchor (or scaffold with rails), and never work up high alone.
Stop everything. First aid, and call 911 for anything serious.

sources: Gail Damerow, Storey's Guide to Raising Chickens, 4th ed. (Storey, 2017)
Gail Damerow, Building Chicken Coops (Storey Country Wisdom Bulletin)
MIA's coop plan and calculator (core/build_calcs.chicken_coop, core/plan_library.py)

standard: Every job meets MIA's standard (a planning phase first, an inspection last, 12 or more steps each with why, hold points, the stop rules its steps call for, two or more sources), and stays drafted until a person confirms it.
